name: HTML & CSS
description: Semantics, the box model, flexbox and grid, specificity, stacking contexts and accessible markup.

modules.name: Semantic HTML & Accessibility
modules.description: Markup that means something — to browsers, to search engines and to assistive technology.

cards.answer: Semantic elements bring built-in behaviour and meaning: keyboard focus and activation, correct roles in the accessibility tree, landmark navigation for screen readers, and better parsing by search engines and reader modes.
cards.explanation: A `<div onclick>` is invisible to keyboard and screen-reader users unless you re-implement `tabindex`, Enter/Space handling, `role` and focus styling — four chances to get it wrong. The native element gets all of that free and correct.

cards.prompt: The first rule of ARIA is: don't use ARIA — use a ___ HTML element instead if one exists.
cards.explanation: ARIA changes only how assistive tech reports an element; it adds no behaviour. `role="button"` on a div still needs manual keyboard handling. Bad ARIA is worse than none because it lies to the accessibility tree.

resources.title: W3C — Using ARIA: rules of ARIA use

cards.prompt: What is wrong with this form field?
cards.answer: No `<label for>` association, and placeholder is not a label — it vanishes on input and often fails contrast. Use `<label for="email">Email</label><input id="email" type="email">`.
cards.explanation: A proper label is announced by screen readers, and clicking it focuses the field — a real usability win on touch. `type="email"` also brings the right mobile keyboard and free validation.

cards.prompt: What are the headline WCAG 2.2 AA requirements developers hit most often?
cards.answer: Contrast of 4.5:1 for normal text (3:1 for large text and UI components), every function reachable by keyboard with a visible focus indicator, text resizable to 200%, correct heading order, alt text for meaningful images, and errors identified in text rather than by colour alone.
cards.explanation: Most of these are testable automatically (axe, Lighthouse) but automation catches perhaps a third of real issues. Tab through the page and use a screen reader once per feature — it finds what scanners cannot.

modules.name: Layout & the Cascade
modules.description: Specificity, box model, flexbox, grid and stacking — the parts that cause the most confusion.

cards.prompt: How is CSS specificity calculated, and what beats it?
cards.answer: As a tuple (inline, ID, class/attribute/pseudo-class, element/pseudo-element), compared left to right. Later rules win ties. `!important` overrides normal declarations, and inline styles beat selectors — but layer order and `!important` in earlier cascade layers can still take precedence.
cards.explanation: The practical lesson is to keep specificity flat: one class per component, no ID selectors in stylesheets, no `!important` arms races. Cascade layers (`@layer`) let you order framework and app styles explicitly instead of by accident.

cards.prompt: How wide is this element rendered, with and without `box-sizing: border-box`?
cards.answer: 244px by default (content-box: 200 + 40 padding + 4 border); exactly 200px with `border-box`.
cards.explanation: `content-box` is the CSS default and almost never what you want, which is why virtually every reset sets `*, *::before, *::after { box-sizing: border-box }`. With border-box, `width` means the visible width.

cards.answer: Flexbox lays out along one axis and sizes from content; Grid defines two-dimensional rows and columns from the container.

left.title: Flexbox
points: One dimension: a row or a column
Ideal for toolbars, button groups, cards in a row

right.title: Grid
points: Layout-in sizing: you define the tracks
Ideal for page layout and complex forms

cards.explanation: They compose — a grid page layout with flex components inside is the normal pattern. `grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(240px, 1fr))` gives a responsive card grid with no media queries at all.

cards.prompt: Your modal has `z-index: 9999` and still renders behind a sidebar. Why?
cards.answer: An ancestor created a stacking context — via `transform`, `opacity < 1`, `filter`, `will-change`, `position` with a z-index, `isolation`, or `contain`. Inside it, z-index is only compared against siblings in that context.
cards.explanation: z-index is not global. Once an ancestor forms a stacking context, no descendant can escape above the ancestor's own level. Fixes: portal the modal to `<body>`, remove the offending property, or use the top-layer `<dialog>` element which sidesteps stacking entirely.

cards.prompt: An animation stutters. Which properties should you animate, and why?
cards.answer: `transform` and `opacity`. They can be handled by the compositor without triggering layout or paint; animating `width`, `top`, `margin` or `box-shadow` forces reflow and repaint every frame.
cards.explanation: The pipeline is style → layout → paint → composite. Layout is the expensive stage, and it invalidates everything after it. Reading a layout property (`offsetHeight`) right after a write forces synchronous layout — the 'layout thrashing' pattern to batch away.

cards.prompt: What do custom properties, `clamp()`, container queries and `:has()` each solve?
cards.answer: Custom properties give runtime-themable values inherited through the tree; `clamp(min, preferred, max)` gives fluid sizing without breakpoints; container queries style by the parent's size rather than the viewport; `:has()` is the long-awaited parent selector.
cards.explanation: Together they remove most of what preprocessors and JavaScript were doing. A component sized with container queries works correctly in a sidebar and in a full-width hero without knowing where it was placed.
